title: PONI Live Debate: AI Integration in NC3
summary: A CSIS debate on whether the US should rely more on AI in nuclear command, control and communications: one side backs AI short of launch authority, the other warns it is too brittle for nuclear decisions.

assertions.quote: It will degrade our decision-making, make the risk of inadvertent escalation more likely, and undermine nuclear stability.

verdicts.note: Most experts judge that automating warning or decision support adds error and speed risks, but no state has disclosed deep integration and the effect is unmeasured.

assertions.quote: AI tools and techniques are already used throughout the almost the entire stack of nuclear command and control.

verdicts.note: Automation and signal processing are long established in US early warning and NC3, but how much modern machine learning is used is not public.
SIPRI says AI has not yet been directly linked to nuclear early-warning efforts, though many nuclear-armed states have explored integrating it, so 'already used across' NC3 overstates the evidence.

WEF says countries are starting to implement AI tools for managing nuclear stockpiles and in some areas of nuclear command, control and communications, which supports use in parts of the system but not 'across' it.

The Bulletin says AI is increasingly applied to military command and control in general, but for nuclear weapons the head of US Strategic Command only called it conceivable that AI will be embedded in decision-support systems, so use across nuclear C3 is not shown as already happening.

assertions.quote: there is no recourse in my mind for AI AI to replace human judgment
AI tools and techniques can actually help to expand the decision space for human decision makers.
there have been literally dozens of nuclear mishaps and near misses in US history.
AI systems are terrible at adapting to novelty.

verdicts.note: Brittleness under distribution shift is a well-documented property of machine-learning systems.

SIPRI notes there is too little historical data on nuclear crises to train AI and doubts LLM-based systems can give sound advice in high-pressure scenarios, which supports the data-limit concern for this setting only.

CNAS notes that AI trained on inadequate data or used outside its design context is often brittle, performing well in the lab and failing dramatically when conditions change, as with self-driving cars.
WEF warns that without humans firmly in the loop, AI platforms may misidentify threats or behave unpredictably in conditions outside their training parameters.

assertions.quote: AI systems can be fooled with clever spoofing attacks. The training data can be poisoned

verdicts.note: Adversarial examples and training-data poisoning are well demonstrated in machine-learning research.

RAND cites numerous demonstrations that small adversarial efforts subvert machine learning with outsized effect, and describes hacking, training-data poisoning and input manipulation that works even without access to the system.
SIPRI says corrupted training data can skew AI decision-support outputs and, because the systems are opaque, lead to dangerous decisions; a cyber operation could manipulate that data deliberately.
WEF says adversaries might use data poisoning, corrupting training data, as a covert weapon to undermine military AI systems; a stated vulnerability rather than a documented attack.

assertions.quote: Humans can over trust AI with catastrophic consequences.

verdicts.note: Automation bias is well documented, including the 2003 Patriot fratricides and driver-assist crashes.
SIPRI says that even when humans keep final authority, operators may come to accept machine outputs uncritically (automation bias), so a human role does not by itself ensure control.
RAND expects commanders to treat a proven AI's suggestions as equal or better than human advice, a potentially unjustified trust, an expert forecast rather than observed behaviour.
CNAS cites the human tendency toward automation bias, plus the history of false alarms from early-warning systems, as reasons a human role does not by itself make AI decision aids safe.
WEF says that even with humans in the loop, cognitive biases shape how AI outputs are read and that in conflict it may be tempting to over-rely on AI systems not yet fit for nuanced decisions.

The Bulletin warns that even if a human is always in the decision loop, a too-heavy dependence on black-box AI systems could present a serious danger, the over-trust mechanism the claim names; expert judgment, not evidence of how often it happens.

assertions.quote: China's nuclear modernization is taking us towards a tripolar nuclear world
affirmed the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons

verdicts.note: Biden and Xi affirmed this in a joint statement at the November 2024 APEC meeting in Lima.
